The daughter lay still on the floor, having fainted. The old woman’s screams and struggles, during which her hair was torn out, changed the orangutan’s probably harmless intentions into rage. With one powerful sweep of its arm, it nearly cut her head from her body. Seeing the blood drove it into a frenzy. Grinding its teeth, its eyes blazing, it sprang upon the girl and dug its dreadful claws into her throat. It held on until she died. At that moment, its wild, wandering eyes caught sight of its master’s face above the head of the bed. He was barely visible, frozen with horror. The animal’s fury instantly turned to fear, no doubt because it remembered the dreaded whip. Seeming to know it deserved punishment, it apparently tried to hide what it had done. It bounded nervously around the room, knocking over and breaking furniture and pulling the mattress from the bed frame. Finally, it seized the daughter’s body and pushed it up the chimney, where it was later found. Then it took the old woman’s body and immediately threw it headfirst through the window.

As the ape approached the window carrying the mutilated body, the terrified sailor retreated to the rod. He slid down it more than climbed and hurried straight home. Fearing the consequences of the slaughter, he gladly forgot any concern for the orangutan. The voices heard by the group on the stairs were the Frenchman’s cries of horror and fear mixed with the animal’s dreadful chattering.

There is little left to tell. The orangutan must have escaped by the rod just before the door was broken open, closing the window as it passed through. Its owner later caught it himself and sold it to the Jardin des Plantes for a large sum. After we explained the events at the Prefect of Police’s office, with a few observations from Dupin, Le Don was released at once. Though the Prefect was friendly toward my companion, he could not quite hide his annoyance at how the case had turned out. He allowed himself one or two sarcastic remarks about the wisdom of everyone minding their own business.

“Let him talk,” said Dupin, who had seen no reason to answer. “Let him say his piece; it will soothe his conscience. I am content to have beaten him on his own ground. His failure to solve this mystery is not nearly as surprising as he thinks, however. The truth is that our friend the Prefect is a little too clever to think deeply.

“In fact, I have not yet named the most important one.”

“What is that, Harry?” the young man asked without energy.

“The obvious comfort: when a woman loses her own admirer, she takes someone else’s. In good society, that always restores her reputation. But really, Dorian, Sibyl Vane must have been very different from the women we usually meet. I think there is something beautiful about her death. I’m glad to live in a century when such wonders occur. They make us believe that romance, passion, and love—the things we all merely play with—can be real.”

“You forget how terribly cruel I was to her.”

“I’m afraid women value cruelty, plain cruelty, more than anything else. Their instincts are remarkably primitive. We have given them freedom, yet they are still slaves searching for masters. They enjoy being ruled. I’m sure you were magnificent. I have never seen you truly furious, but I can imagine how lovely you looked. Besides, you said something two days ago that I dismissed as a flight of fancy. Now I see it was completely true and explains everything.”

“What did I say, Harry?”

“That Sibyl Vane stood for every romantic heroine in your eyes. One night she was Desdemona, another Ophelia. She died as Juliet and came back to life as Imogen.”

“She will never come back to life now,” he muttered, covering his face with his hands.

“No, never. Her last performance is over. But you must see that lonely death in the cheap, showy dressing room as a strange, darkly vivid piece of a Jacobean tragedy, a wonderful scene from Webster, Ford, or Cyril Tourneur. She never really lived, so she never really died. To you, at least, she was a dream, a ghost passing through Shakespeare’s plays and making them lovelier. She was a reed through which his music sounded richer and happier. When she encountered actual life, she damaged it, and it damaged her, and so she died. Grieve for Ophelia if you want. Put ashes on your head because Cordelia was strangled. Cry out against heaven over the death of Brabantio’s daughter. But do not waste tears on Sibyl Vane. Those women are more real than she was.”

Neither spoke. The evening grew darker inside the room. Shadows crept silently from the garden on silver feet, and the colors slowly faded from everything, as if tired.

After some time, Dorian Gray looked up.

“What’s wrong?”

I said:

“Dad and Mom and my sister, and—”

Then I broke down. He said:

“Oh, damn it, don’t cry like that. Everyone has troubles, and this will work out. What’s happened to them?”

“They’re—they’re—are you the boat’s watchman?”

“Yes,” he said, sounding rather pleased with himself. “I’m the captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and chief deckhand. Sometimes I’m the cargo and passengers too. I’m not as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be so generous to every Tom, Dick, and Harry, throwing money around like he does. But I’ve told him many times I wouldn’t trade places with him. A sailor’s life is the life for me, I say. I’d be damned if I’d live two miles outside town, where nothing ever happens, for all his money and twice as much besides. I tell him—”

I interrupted:

“They’re in terrible trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Dad, Mom, my sister, and Miss Hooker. If you could take your ferry up there—”

“Up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“Which wreck?”

“There’s only one.”

“What, you mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good heavens! What are they doing there?”

“Well, they didn’t go there on purpose.”

“I should think not! They haven’t a chance unless they get off quickly. How on earth did they land in such a mess?”

“It was easy enough. Miss Hooker was visiting that town upriver—”

“Yes, Booth’s Landing. Go on.”

“She was visiting Booth’s Landing. Around dusk she and her Black servant set out on the horse ferry to spend the night at a friend’s house, Miss What’s-her-name—I forget. They lost their steering oar, swung around, and drifted downstream backward for about two miles. Then they hit the wreck and folded over it. The ferryman, the servant, and the horses all drowned, but Miss Hooker grabbed hold and climbed aboard the wreck. About an hour after dark, we came down in our trading boat. It was so dark we didn’t see the wreck until we hit it, and our boat folded over it too. Everyone escaped except Bill Whipple. Oh, he was the best fellow! I almost wish it had been me instead.”

“My goodness! I’ve never heard anything to beat that.
